I'm a resident of Burlington, VT, and while Sanders has represented Vermont for a long time (at least parts of it) and therefor knows what kind of a gun culture exists in the state, he's going to inevitably change his stance to fit the wider geographical area. Vermont has a pretty low gun crime rate for the number of guns in the state. I have four. Three of them are semi-automatic, and none of them fall under Sanders' definition of guns that people should have. I have no plans to ever have to shoot at anyone (I don't even hunt), and I know that everyone else I know who owns guns thinks much the same way. There isn't any gang activity, break-ins are few and far between, and aside from the Rutland corridor to Montreal for heroin, there isn't even that much Big Drug activity in the state, so there aren't many people who would use guns against other people. What's good for the goose isn't necessarily good for the gander, and Sanders should know that. What we have in Vermont is working. What we have in Vermont WOULDN'T work in most other states, though, so a cover-all ban on semi-auto weapons would not work everywhere, but neither would more lax gun laws. Different strokes for different folks.

Then again, this might be a campaign promise to garner votes from the sort of people who don't own guns, don't know anyone who own guns, and have never been shooting. You know, the sort of people who are terrified of them because they see massacres on the news, and think that it's going to happen to them one of these days while they sit in their living room. They're fundamentally against guns, and are irrationally afraid of them? Whether Sanders follows up on it remains to be seen.

I'm not a single issue voter, and since I've already got my guns, I'm not going to turn them in no matter what legislation goes through. I think that campaign finance reform, workers' rights and (directly regarding Trump) negotiation tact is more important than what Sanders may or may not do regarding guns. I like the fact that he has a consistently un-erring moral sense when it comes to his voting history, and that he isn't party to corporate donations like sHillary is. I know that he's an asshole in person, but in terms of a politician, I could barely ask for a better candidate from the ones that are out there.

Regarding gun reform, I think that as a country, we've doing a damn good job of preventing gun deaths for the number of guns in the country. Yeah, there's a massacre here and there, but there are a lot more factors than just guns. Mental health needs to be destigmatized and free. What sort of country can seriously call itself the greatest country in the world while it can't even keep its citizens healthy? In other countries that have more strict gun laws and similar healthcare systems, the same sort of killings happen, but without guns. Suicides account for the vast majority of "gun crime", but those suicides are going to happen whether or not people have guns. Japan has a comparable number of suicides, but they're jumping off of buildings and hanging themselves because they don't have access to guns. Guns are an easy scapegoat, not the cause of all of our problems. Some part of me thinks that Sanders knows that, but saying "no semi-auto guns" is easier than explaining more complex solutions to crowds of people who have been weaned onto soundbites and tweets.

I'm on Sanders' email list, so I saw when he called for the ban, and I was pissed when I saw it. That being said, no politician is going to be perfect in anyone's mind, so I'm prepared to concede this point. Even if he is elected, he still has to get something like this through Congress, and an executive order is going to be scrutinized immediately because of the magnitude of the decision. I don't care what the NRA gave Sanders as a rating, up until that email, many of his policies regarding guns made perfect sense (keeping the waiting period at three days, protecting gun sellers from the crimes that customers commit, fixing star-sale laws, instant background checks, guns in checked baggage, preventing the UN from binding US citizens to UN gun laws, more). Some of them didn't, like the 10-round "high-cap" limit (which is bullshit).

I'm not a member of the NRA because of the process they use to support politicians, but I do recognize that they are made up of American opinions that people feel strongly about. It isn't a nameless, faceless organization that's supported by corporate interests that thwarts popular opinion. The NRA isn't something "to be defeated", and it isn't going anywhere. Even if some legislation bans guns, there will still be the NRA, and they'll still support gun rights, even if it's just to get them back.

Cologne police seemingly withheld information about New Year's Eve suspects' country of origin based on 2008 guideline from NRW department of the interior (translation in comments)

„As it was 'politically delicate', the Cologne police has not disclosed the country of origin of the suspects in its press release for New Year's Eve. It apparently acted on order of the department of the interior.

Cologne. It appears that it was not the own decision of the Cologne police to not name the county of origin of the New Year's Eve suspects. According to information available to the Kölner Stattanzeiger, the police rather has followed a general precept of Northrhine-Westphalia's department of the interior.

The respective circular decree, which is available to the newspaper, originates from 2008 and is binding for all police departments in the federal state. Under the headline 'Guidelines for the NRW State Police for the Protection of National Minorities against Discrimination', the ministry orders all departments to avoid 'the use of all phrases in both internal and external use' which 'could be abused, re-functioned, or interpreted by third parties to downgrade humans'.

In his first internal report regarding the events of New Year's Eve, the chief of the of the Cologne police control center allegedly did intentionally not name the origin of the suspects, as he considered this to be too 'politically delicate'.

The paper also gives the police directions dictating in which cases the public is to be informed over the origin of criminals or suspects. Following from this, such information is only to be made public if 'there is a broad public interest or if this would help with the search for criminals in individual cases'

The NRW secretary of the interior, Ralf Jäger (SPD), has stated that he 'firmly urged' the Cologne police to release information regarding the culprits' country of origin to the public if available on the days following New Year's Eve – even if the culprits are refugees. However, the former police superintendend of Cologne, Wolfgang Albers (who has been forced into retirement by Jäger), only followed these instructions on January 4th during a press conference.

At the same time, its own observations and that of eyewitnesses meant that the police already had clear evidence on New Year's Eve itself which showed that the suspects were primarily young men from North-Africa and Arabic states.“

While it is understandably difficult to gauge your actions, thoughts, words, and intentions with some "cosmic scale" that lets you know that you're doing it "right", I think testing out some of the ideas of compassion and community aren't harmful to the development of the common man.

That being said, whoever Jesus was (or wasn't) is a pretty a cool guy, in principle. I don't see anything wrong with looking at an idea and trying to use it to bring actual joy and compassion to other beings, here and now. I honestly hope we come to a time where religion becomes more of a philosophy; rationally pondered, but not considered to be something to get into an existential crisis over. You may find some of Nietzsche, Twain, or Poe to be particularly dark, but it would honestly be considered a mental illness if you seriously devoted yourself to their personage.

Devotion and rational consideration are two different ways to approach the same subject, but I think each produces wildly contrasting results.
